children: The District of Columbia Court of Appeals said in a

that lawyers for a Deutsche Bank subsidiary in a mortgage foreclosure lawsuit cited nonexistent cases generated by artificial intelligence, calling the matter a "cautionary tale" about lawyers' misuse of AI.

The appeals court, the highest local court in Washington, said it discovered that a brief from Deutsche Bank National Trust “contained multiple citations to cases that the court was unable to locate or confirm as legitimate.” Deutsche Bank National Trust was involved in the case as the trustee for a securitized mortgage trust.

An outside lawyer for Deutsche Bank, Loishirl Hall, apologized in a court filing and said she used a Google artificial intelligence program to help prepare the brief. She said she had taken steps to verify the accuracy of citations before they were submitted to the court.

The appeals court said Hall took ownership of her error, but "every firm attorney who signed the brief bears some responsibility." Hall’s firm at the time, McCabe, Weisberg & Conway, told the appeals court that it does not allow its employees to use AI for “drafting of any legal correspondence or documents.” Hall and Deutsche Bank did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The McCabe firm also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The D.C. Court of Appeals said the case was the first in which it encountered a brief containing fabricated citations. The legal industry’s use of AI is so commonplace now, the court said, that “attorneys can no longer credibly claim ignorance of its pitfalls, including its propensity to hallucinate legal authority.”

“Our intent is not to discourage attorneys from using AI — indeed, we have reached a point where attorneys eschew at least an understanding, if not use, of AI at their own peril — but to emphasize the importance of doing so discerningly and responsibly,” the panel of judges said.
The court struck Deutsche Bank National Trust’s brief and said it was referring the matter to the D.C. attorney discipline arm for “any investigation it deems appropriate."

Judge Stephen Glickman, writing separately, said striking the court filing is an “appropriate but comparatively weak response that unfortunately penalizes the innocent client for its counsel’s offense.” Glickman suggested the full appeals court may “wish to address this situation.”
